title: What Will Give Students Ambition?
author: Dominic Salles
summary: Dominic Salles answers a school leader's LinkedIn question about how to lift ambition in a middle-attaining cohort that is content with grade 4s and 5s. He responds with eight practical levers rather than a single inspirational fix. These range from tracking progress against attendance, to making a public fuss of a standard most pupils can reach, to codifying values with a curriculum that actually builds them. He also covers retrieval and worked examples, aspiration visits, and the use of Progress 8 data in middle-leader meetings. The closing move is cultural: share the causes of success across colleagues and never single out low performers for blame.
points: Show students their progress, effort and attendance on one spreadsheet so they see the link between what they put in and what they get out.
Set a progress standard that over half the cohort can reach and celebrate it loudly, so a social norm does the motivating.
Stated values such as ambition only count if the school builds a curriculum and offer that develops them.
Use class-level Progress 8 data in department meetings to find unexpectedly successful colleagues and spread their methods without blaming the weakest.
quotes: Make a big deal about progress - although it is controversial for many teachers, when you league table students' progress they are much more likely to be motivated to succeed.

The key here is to make a massive fuss of anyone reaching a particular standard - and you want that standard to be something that more than 50% of the class or cohort will reach, as that will establish a social norm. The social norm will act as peer pressure to succeed.
Many schools codify these: ambition, responsibility, respect, kindness, etc. But fewer ask how they will make sure students develop these.

But visits from ex students who have got into university courses they really want, and visits to universities are powerful, especially as so much capital investment has gone into them in the last decade.
Everyone wants to get great progress, and this is a mechanism which will stop teachers saying 'it's because the kids don't work hard enough'. This answer is always true!

This only works if those with low progress are never singled out for blame - their low progress needs to be an internal signal to them that they have much to gain from whichever colleague is sharing the causes of their success.
